chapter.title: Events, Threads and Tasks
chapter.para: .NET calls back: when a timer fires, when a task runs, when a window is clicked. A Rexx method is given to .NET as a handler, .net~handler(object, message), and runs either at once on .NET's thread, or queued, on a Rexx thread of the program's choosing.

section.title: A Timer, Handled in a Loop
section.para: You want to react to .NET's events one at a time, on one thread.

example.title: A Timer, Handled in a Loop
example.programlisting:
clock = .Clock~new timer = .net~System~Timers~Timer~new(30) timer~Elapsed += .net~handler(clock, "TICK", "queued") timer~Start .net~eventLoop -- the ticks run here, one by one timer~Stop; timer~Dispose say "done after" clock~ticks "ticks"
::requires "net.cls" ::class Clock ::attribute ticks ::method init expose ticks ticks = 0 ::method tick expose ticks use arg sender, e ticks += 1 say "tick" ticks if ticks = 3 then .net~stopEventLoop
example.screen: tick 1 tick 2 tick 3 done after 3 ticks

section.para: How it works. timer~Elapsed += handler adds a handler to the event, as in C#. With the option queued, each call waits in a queue, and .net~eventLoop runs them on this thread, in order, until .net~stopEventLoop: the handler needs no care about threads. Without it, the handler would run at once on .NET's thread pool.
See also Reference, Callbacks, Events and Tasks.

section.title: Work on .NET's Thread Pool
section.para: You want to run Rexx methods in parallel, and to wait for .NET's asynchronous methods.

example.title: Work on .NET's Thread Pool
example.programlisting:
tasks = .array~new do i = 1 to 3 w = .Worker~new(i) tasks~append(.net~System~Threading~Tasks~Task~Run(.net~as(.net~handler(w, "WORK"), "System.Func<int>"))) end all = .net~System~Threading~Tasks~Task~WhenAll(tasks) -- a Task<int[]> say all~await~makeString("L", " ") t = .net~System~IO~File~WriteAllTextAsync(.net~System~IO~Path~GetTempFileName, "x") t~await say t~IsCompletedSuccessfully
::requires "net.cls" ::class Worker ::method init expose n use arg n ::method work unguarded expose n call SysSleep 0.1 return n * n

section.para: How it works. Task.Run runs a handler on .NET's thread pool. A handler fits Task.Run(Action) first, which has no result: .net~as(handler, "System.Func<int>") chooses the overload that returns one. Task.WhenAll waits for several, and ~await blocks until a task ends and gives its result (here an array of the three). The worker's method is UNGUARDED, so that the three run at once. WriteAllTextAsync, as every asynchronous .NET method, returns a task to await.
See also Reference, Callbacks, Events and Tasks, Tasks.

section.title: Updating from Another Thread
section.para: You want a worker thread that reports to the thread that owns the display.

example.title: Updating from Another Thread
example.programlisting:
reporter = .Reporter~new reporter~start("WORK") -- another Rexx thread .net~eventLoop -- this one is the event thread say "last shown:" reporter~shown "of 50"
::requires "net.cls" ::class Reporter ::attribute shown ::method work unguarded -- (guarded, SHOW would wait for it) do i = 1 to 50 .NetEventThread~runLaterLatest(self, "SHOW", "I", i) end .NetEventThread~runLater(self, "DONE") ::method show expose shown use arg shown ::method done .net~stopEventLoop

section.para: How it works. A window belongs to the thread that made it, and only that thread may touch it: other threads send it messages with runLater (BSF4ooRexx's model). Here there is no window, so the event thread is the Rexx thread in .net~eventLoop, and the same code works with one. runLaterLatest replaces a waiting message of the same kind, so a fast worker does not flood the display: of the 50 reports, a few run, the last one always. The worker's method is UNGUARDED: guarded, it would hold the object while it runs, and show, on the event thread, would wait for it for ever.
The samples windows/forms-progress.rex and windows/forms-two-threads.rex do the same with windows.
See also Reference, The Event Thread.
